title: Batch composting versus continuous composting: which to choose
subtitle: Understanding how the two methods work and which fits your garden's waste pattern
excerpt: Batch composting fills a bay all at once and leaves it to mature, producing ready compost in 4–8 weeks with a managed hot phase. Continuous composting adds material over time to a single bin and harvests from the bottom, taking 6–18 months. Neither is better in all cases — the choice depends on how your waste arrives.
sourceNotes: WRAP home composting guidance; RHS composting advice; US Composting Council hot and cold composting comparison.

glossaryTerms.definition: A composting method where the heap is managed to reach and maintain temperatures of 55–70°C, which kills weed seeds and pathogens and breaks down material in 4–8 weeks.
A slow composting method where material is added to a heap or bin over time without active temperature management, breaking down over 6–18 months.

content.text: Batch composting collects all your material at once — a lawn mow, a border clear-out, a delivery of horse manure — builds the heap in one session, and leaves it alone to mature.

You have large volumes of material arriving in pulses: grass mowings, autumn leaves, a hedge trim, a stable delivery of horse manure. These are natural batch inputs.
You want to kill weed seeds. A batch that reaches 55°C for 3 consecutive days (with turning) kills most annual weed seeds. A cold continuous bin does not.
You want finished compost on a predictable timeline — 4–8 weeks for a well-managed hot batch versus 6–18 months for a cold continuous bin.
You have a steady trickle of kitchen waste and small amounts of garden material arriving daily. This is the most common domestic situation.
You do not want to manage the process: no turning schedule, no temperature monitoring, minimal thought.
You have limited space and cannot justify two or three bays.
The hybrid — most gardens use both

A standard two-bay or three-bay system uses the batch method: the first bay fills over several weeks and then rests while the second bay fills. This is not quite a pure batch (material arrives over days not all at once) but is close enough to generate some heat and produces compost in 3–6 months.

Adding a black dalek bin to a batch setup provides a continuous outlet for daily kitchen waste that is not part of the hot heap. The kitchen bin feeds the dalek; the seasonal garden material feeds the hot bay.

rows.symptom: Batch heap never reaches 45°C despite sufficient volume
rows.cause: Material arrived over too long a period — the first-in material has cooled before enough new material arrives to sustain heat
rows.fix: For the next batch, collect and store material until you have at least 0.5 m³ before building the heap in one session.
